verses.zh: 过了两年，法老做梦，梦见自己站在河边，
verses.en: At the end of two full years[NOTE:1] Pharaoh had a dream.[NOTE:2] As he was standing by the Nile,
notes: Heb “two years, days.”
Heb “was dreaming.”
verses.commentary:
41:1 "at the end of two full years" This, of course, relates to chapter 40, where Joseph interprets
two person's dreams, both hoping to be released from prison, and yet, this was not successful. The date is
from the restoration of one servant and the execution of the other. Throughout the account of Joseph it is
interesting that the author/editor gives us several dates:

- he was seventeen years old when he was sold into slavery (cf. Gen. 37:2)

- he became second in command of the nation of Egypt when he was thirty years old (cf. Gen. 41:46)

With these figures it is possible to see that he had remained in jail approximately thirteen
years. This is conditioned on how much time he stayed in Potiphar's service before the incident with his
wife.

▣ "Pharaoh" Pharaoh is a collective title for all of the kings of Egypt as Hadad was for Syria,
Caesar later becomes for Rome, and Czar was for Russia. The etymology of the term is uncertain, but most
Egyptologists assume it is from the phrase "the great house" (BDB 829, i.e., the house of the gods). There
has been much speculation about when Joseph could have arisen as second in command over all of Egypt. Many
assume that it had to be during the Hyksos period known as "the Shepherd Kings," who were apparently Semitic,
not Egyptian (see AB, p. 316). They ruled from 1730 to 1570 B.C. However, it is interesting
that in Gen. 41:1, the term for "river," which obviously refers to the Nile, is found in a form that only
occurs during the 18th Dynasty or 1546-1085 B.C. From Egyptian documents we also learn that
throughout the history of Egypt, there were Semites in places of responsibility in many other Egyptian
dynasties than the two mentioned above.

▣ "a dream" There is extensive literature, both in Egypt and Mesopotamia, concerning dreams and
their interpretation. It is interesting that the two Hebrew persons involved in interpreting dreams each
worked for pagan kings

- Daniel in Mesopotamia

- Joseph in Egypt

The NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 154, makes an interesting comment about the three kinds of dreams.

- natural sleep, Ps. 126:1; Isa. 29:7-8; Eccl. 5:7

- false revelation, Jer. 23:25,27,32; 27:9-10; 29:8; Zech. 10:2

- true revelation, Gen. 20:3; 28:12; Num. 12:6; 1 Kgs. 3:5; Dan. 2:28; Matt. 1:20

Visions can often occur at night, but seem to be different from dreams. The exact nature of
the difference is not stated. YHWH communicates to a person's subconscious using symbols and metaphors with
which they are familiar.

▣ "the Nile" This (BDB 384) is the first in a series of uniquely Egyptian terms. Not only are
they uniquely Egyptian terms, but the entire context is culturally Egyptian. This river and its annual flood
was the source of Egypt's life and fertility. It was considered a god (cf. Exod. 1:22) to be appeased.

verses.zh: 有七只母牛从河里上来，又美好又肥壮，在芦荻中吃草。
verses.en: seven fine-looking, fat cows were coming up out of the Nile,[NOTE:1] and they grazed in the reeds.
notes: Heb “And look, he was standing by the Nile, and look, from the Nile were coming up seven cows, attractive of appearance and fat of flesh.” By the use of the particle הִנֵּה (hinneh, “look”), the narrator invites the audience to see the dream through Pharaoh’s eyes.
verses.commentary:
41:2 "seven cows" We learn from Plutarch, the Roman historian, and Clement of Alexandria, an early
church father, that a "cow" (BDB 831) symbolized the bounty of the earth in Egypt. The cow was the main herd
animal in Egypt, as sheep were in Palestine. The cow was an obvious choice in an Egyptian dream concerning
agricultural bounty (i.e., "sleek," BDB 421 [lit. "beautiful"] and "fat," BDB 135).

▣ "they grazed in the marsh grass" This is another Egyptian loan word. We know from Egyptian
sources that the cattle immersed themselves in the water along the Nile for several reasons:

- to keep cool

- to keep the insects off

- to eat the lush growth of marsh grass (BDB 28)

verses.zh: 随后又有七只母牛从河里上来，又丑陋又干瘦，与那七只母牛一同站在河边。
verses.en: Then seven bad-looking, thin cows were coming up after them from the Nile,[NOTE:1] and they stood beside the other cows at the edge of the river.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “And look, seven other cows were coming up after them from the Nile, bad of appearance and thin of flesh.”
Heb “the Nile.” This has been replaced by “the river” in the translation for stylistic reasons.
verses.commentary:
41:3-4 These cows are in direct contrast with the healthy cows of Gen. 41:2.

- ugly (lit. "bad of sight"), BDB 948 I CONSTRUCT BDB 909

- gaunt (lit. "thin of flesh"), BDB 201 CONSTRUCT BDB 142

They eat up (BDB 37, KB 46, Qal IMPERFECT with waw) the healthy cows
(Gen. 41:4).

verses.zh: 这又丑陋又干瘦的七只母牛吃尽了那又美好又肥壮的七只母牛。法老就醒了。
verses.en: The bad-looking, thin cows ate the seven fine-looking, fat cows. Then Pharaoh woke up.

verses.zh: 他又睡着，第二回做梦，梦见一棵麦子长了七个穗子，又肥大又佳美，
verses.en: Then he fell asleep again and had a second dream: There were seven heads of grain growing[NOTE:1] on one stalk, healthy[NOTE:2] and good.
notes: Heb “coming up.”
Heb “fat.”
verses.commentary:
41:5 The second dream is repetitious except the cows are replaced by contrasting ears of grain
(BDB 987 II).

verses.zh: 随后又长了七个穗子，又细弱又被东风吹焦了。
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] seven heads of grain, thin and burned by the east wind, were sprouting up after them.
notes: Heb “And look.”
verses.commentary:
41:6 "the east wind" This desert wind (BDB 870), so notorious for its blighting of the agricultural
produce of the land, is called the "Sirroco" (Aramaic) in Palestine, where it blows from the southeast. It
is called the "Khamsin" in Egypt and it comes more from the south, southeast. It is referred to in
Ezek. 17:10 and Hosea 13:15. All the food for the cattle (and thereby humans) would die.

verses.zh: 这细弱的穗子吞了那七个又肥大又饱满的穗子。法老醒了，不料是个梦。
verses.en: The thin heads swallowed up the seven healthy and full heads. Then Pharaoh woke up and realized it was a dream.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “And look, a dream.”sn Pharaoh’s two dreams, as explained in the following verses, pertained to the economy of Egypt. Because of the Nile River, the land of Egypt weathered all kinds of famines—there was usually grain in Egypt, and if there was grain and water the livestock would flourish. These two dreams, however, indicated that poverty would overtake plenty and that the blessing of the herd and the field would cease.

verses.zh: 到了早晨，法老心里不安，就差人召了埃及所有的术士和博士来；法老就把所做的梦告诉他们，却没有人能给法老圆解。
verses.en: In the morning he[NOTE:1] was troubled, so he called for[NOTE:2] all the diviner-priests[NOTE:3] of Egypt and all its wise men. Pharaoh told them his dreams,[NOTE:4] but no one could interpret[NOTE:5] them for him.[NOTE:6]
notes: Heb “his spirit.”
Heb “he sent and called,” which indicates an official summons.
The Hebrew term חַרְטֹם (khartom) is an Egyptian loanword (hyr-tp) that describes a class of priests who were skilled in such interpretations.

The Hebrew text has the singular (though Smr reads the plural). If retained, the singular must be collective for the set of dreams. Note the plural pronoun “them,” referring to the dreams, in the next clause. However, note that in v. 15 Pharaoh uses the singular to refer to the two dreams. In vv. 17-24 Pharaoh seems to treat the dreams as two parts of one dream (see especially v. 22).
“there was no interpreter.”
Heb “for Pharaoh.” The pronoun “him” has been used in the translation for stylistic reasons.
verses.commentary:
41:8 "his spirit was troubled" The term translated "spirit" is ruah (BDB 924;
SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT IN THE
BIBLE), which denotes the life force of animals and humans on this planet. It can be translated "wind,"
"breath," and "spirit."

The VERB "troubled" (BDB 821, KB 952, Niphal IMPERFECT with
waw) is a rare word. It is used in the Niphal stem in Ps. 77:4; Dan. 2:1,3, and the Qal
is used of God's Spirit "stirring" in Jdg. 13:25. Its basic meaning is "to thrust" or "to impel."

▣ "the magicians of Egypt" This seems to be another Egyptian loan word that comes from the root
"to engrave" (BDB 355) and is always used of occultic knowledge (cf. Exod. 7:11,22; 8:7,18,19; 9:11). Why an
Egyptian term would be used for Babylonian soothsaying priests (cf. Dan. 1:20; 2:2,10,27; 4:7,9; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: MAGIC) is
uncertain. Therefore, these men were the readers, practitioners, and writers of the ancient books concerning
divination, interpretations, etc. They are referred to not only in Egypt, but also in Babylon (cf. Is. 44:25;
Jer. 50:35; 51:57) and in Persia (cf. Esther 1:13 and 6:13). The terms used in Daniel are different terms,
but refer to the same type of people.

For an extensive discussion of the practices of divination and dream interpretation see
A. L. Oppenheim, The Interpretation of Dreams in the Ancient Near East, pp. 184-307.

▣ "and all its wise men" This refers to the court counselors (BDB 481 CONSTRUCT
BDB 314, cf. Exod. 7:11; Isa. 19:11,12), not necessarily the priestly class of soothsayers referred to by
the former term.

▣ "there was no one who could interpret them to Pharaoh" Pharaoh apparently had more honest
wise men than Nebuchadnezzar, who did not trust his magi enough to give them the content of his dreams lest
they make up an interpretation (cf. Daniel 2)!

verses.zh: 那时酒政对法老说：「我今日想起我的罪来。
verses.en: Then the chief cupbearer said to Pharaoh, “Today I recall my failures.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “sins, offenses.” He probably refers here to the offenses that landed him in prison (see 40:1).
verses.commentary:
41:9-12 "my own offenses" This paragraph refers to the events recorded in Genesis 40. It almost
seems he is talking to a new Pharaoh.

verses.zh: 从前法老恼怒臣仆，把我和膳长下在护卫长府内的监里。
verses.en: Pharaoh was enraged with his servants, and he put me in prison in the house of the captain of the guards—me and the chief baker.

verses.zh: 我们二人同夜各做一梦，各梦都有讲解。
verses.en: We each had a dream one night; each of us had a dream with its own meaning.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “and we dreamed a dream in one night, I and he, each according to the interpretation of his dream we dreamed.”

verses.zh: 在那里同着我们有一个希伯来的少年人，是护卫长的仆人，我们告诉他，他就把我们的梦圆解，是按着各人的梦圆解的。
verses.en: Now a young man, a Hebrew, a servant[NOTE:1] of the captain of the guards,[NOTE:2] was with us there. We told him our dreams,[NOTE:3] and he interpreted the meaning of each of our respective dreams for us.[NOTE:4]
notes: Or “slave.”
Heb “a servant to the captain of the guards.” On this construction see GKC 419-20 §129.c.
The words “our dreams” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “and he interpreted for us our dreams, each according to his dream he interpreted.”
verses.commentary: 41:12 "a Hebrew youth" See note at Gen. 40:15.

verses.zh: 后来正如他给我们圆解的成就了：我官复原职，膳长被挂起来了。
verses.en: It happened just as he had said[NOTE:1] to us—Pharaoh[NOTE:2] restored me to my office, but he impaled the baker.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “interpreted.”
Heb “he”; the referent (Pharaoh) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “him”; the referent (the baker) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
verses.commentary:
41:13 "hanged him" See SPECIAL
TOPIC: HANG

verses.zh: 法老遂即差人去召约瑟，他们便急忙带他出监，他就剃头，刮脸，换衣裳，进到法老面前。
verses.en: Then Pharaoh summoned[NOTE:1] Joseph. So they brought him quickly out of the dungeon; he shaved himself, changed his clothes, and came before Pharaoh.
notes: Heb “and Pharaoh sent and called,” indicating a summons to the royal court.
verses.commentary:
41:14 "they hurriedly brought him out of the dungeon" Again we have an Egyptian loan word (see note
at Gen. 40:15) in the term "dungeon," which seems to mean "incarcerated within an Egyptian fortress."
Apparently Joseph was kept with the political prisoners.

▣ "shaved himself and changed his clothes" Here again is the Egyptian custom of not only shaving
one's beard, but of shaving one's entire body, and cleaning one's self completely before approaching
Pharaoh.

verses.zh: 法老对约瑟说：「我做了一梦，没有人能解；我听见人说，你听了梦就能解。」
verses.en: Pharaoh said to Joseph, “I had a dream,[NOTE:1] and there is no one who can interpret[NOTE:2] it. But I have heard about you, that[NOTE:3] you can interpret dreams.”[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “dreamed a dream.”
Heb “there is no one interpreting.”
Heb “saying.”
Heb “you hear a dream to interpret it,” which may mean, “you only have to hear a dream to be able to interpret it.”

verses.zh: 约瑟回答法老说：「这不在乎我，　神必将平安的话回答法老。」
verses.en: Joseph replied to Pharaoh, “It is not within my power,[NOTE:1] but God will speak concerning[NOTE:2] the welfare of Pharaoh.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “not within me.”
Heb “God will answer.”

The expression שְׁלוֹם פַּרְעֹה (shelom parʿoh) is here rendered “the welfare of Pharaoh” because the dream will be about life in his land. Some interpret it to mean an answer of “peace”—one that will calm his heart, or give him the answer that he desires (cf. NIV, NRSV, NLT).
verses.commentary:
41:16 "It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh a favorable answer" This answer is much like Dan. 2:27-30.
Joseph knew the source of his dreams was not in his ability to use divination or to read ancient documents,
but in the power of God (cf. Gen. 40:8). Joseph has a theocentric worldview (cf. Gen. 41:25,28,32).

The term translated "favorable" is the term shalom (BDB 1022), which denotes "peace,"
"well being," or "favor." See
SPECIAL TOPIC: PEACE
(SHALOM). In the context of chapter 41, the shalom may refer to Pharaoh's spirit ("his
spirit was troubled") in Gen. 41:8.

verses.zh: 法老对约瑟说：「我梦见我站在河边，
verses.en: Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, “In my dream I was standing[NOTE:1] by the edge of the Nile.
notes: Heb “In my dream look, I was standing.” The use of the particle הִנֵּה (hinneh, “look”) here (and also in vv. 18, 19, 22, 23) invites the hearer (within the context of the narrative, Joseph, but in the broader sense the reader or hearer of the Book of Genesis) to observe the scene through Pharaoh’s eyes.
verses.commentary:
41:17-24 This is a slightly different form from the account of Pharaoh's dream found earlier in
chapter 41. It fits the situation exactly. No one would retell the story exactly the same without
embellishing some points and omitting other points. To me it is a sign of the historicity of the account.

verses.zh: 有七只母牛从河里上来，又肥壮又美好，在芦荻中吃草。
verses.en: Then seven fat and fine-looking cows were coming up out of the Nile, and they grazed in the reeds.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “and look, from the Nile seven cows were coming up, fat of flesh and attractive of appearance, and they grazed in the reeds.”
verses.commentary:
41:18 The term "sleek" is a Hebrew CONSTRUCT "beautiful" (BDB 421) and "form"
(BDB 1061). This CONSTRUCT is used of

- cows, here

- women, Gen. 29:17; Deut. 21:11; 1 Sam. 25:3; Esther 2:7

- man, Gen. 39:6

- tree, Jer. 11:16

verses.zh: 随后又有七只母牛上来，又软弱又丑陋又干瘦，在埃及遍地，我没有见过这样不好的。
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] seven other cows came up after them; they were scrawny, very bad looking, and lean. I had never seen such bad-looking cows[NOTE:2] as these in all the land of Egypt!
notes: Heb “And look.”
The word “cows” is supplied here in the translation for stylistic reasons.

verses.zh: 这又干瘦又丑陋的母牛吃尽了那以先的七只肥母牛，
verses.en: The lean, bad-looking cows ate up the seven[NOTE:1] fat cows.
notes: Heb “the seven first fat cows.”

verses.zh: 吃了以后却看不出是吃了，那丑陋的样子仍旧和先前一样。我就醒了。
verses.en: When they had eaten them,[NOTE:1] no one would have known[NOTE:2] that they had done so, for they were just as bad looking as before. Then I woke up.
notes: Heb “when they went inside them.”
Heb “it was not known.”

verses.zh: 我又梦见一棵麦子，长了七个穗子，又饱满又佳美，
verses.en: I also saw in my dream[NOTE:1] seven heads of grain growing on one stalk, full and good.
notes: Heb “and I saw in my dream and look.”

verses.zh: 随后又长了七个穗子，枯槁细弱，被东风吹焦了。
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] seven heads of grain, withered and thin and burned with the east wind, were sprouting up after them.
notes: Heb “And look.”

verses.zh: 这些细弱的穗子吞了那七个佳美的穗子。我将这梦告诉了术士，却没有人能给我解说。」
verses.en: The thin heads of grain swallowed up the seven good heads of grain. So I told all this[NOTE:1] to the diviner-priests, but no one could tell me its meaning.”[NOTE:2]
notes: The words “all this” have been supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “and there was no one telling me.”
verses.commentary:
41:24 "magicians" See SPECIAL
TOPIC: MAGIC

verses.zh: 约瑟对法老说：「法老的梦乃是一个。　神已将所要做的事指示法老了。
verses.en: Then Joseph said to Pharaoh, “Both dreams of Pharaoh have the same meaning.[NOTE:1] God has revealed[NOTE:2] to Pharaoh what he is about to do.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “the dream of Pharaoh is one.”
Heb “declared.”
The active participle here indicates what is imminent.
verses.commentary:
41:25 Joseph is addressing an Egyptian who would not recognize YHWH so he used the more general name
for Deity, Elohim. See
SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR
DEITY, C.

This God is ready and willing to inform Pharaoh, a pagan king, about His future plans
(cf. Gen. 41:25,28,32). The "nations" have always been the focus of God's eternal, redemptive plan
(cf. Gen. 3:15; 12:3; Exod. 19:5-6; Isaiah; Jonah; Matt. 28:19-20; Luke 24:47; Acts 1:8)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL
REDEMPTIVE PLAN

verses.zh: 七只好母牛是七年，七个好穗子也是七年；这梦乃是一个。
verses.en: The seven good cows represent seven years, and the seven good heads of grain represent seven years. Both dreams have the same meaning.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “one dream it is.”
verses.commentary:
41:26-32 Joseph began to explain the dream to Pharaoh. Note in Gen. 41:24 none of his magicians
could do it.

41:26 "seven years" In literature of the ANE seven year cycles were common (cf. ANET, p. 31).

verses.zh: 那随后上来的七只又干瘦又丑陋的母牛是七年，那七个虚空、被东风吹焦的穗子也是七年，都是七个荒年。
verses.en: The seven lean, bad-looking cows that came up after them represent seven years, as do the seven empty heads of grain burned with the east wind. They represent[NOTE:1] seven years of famine.
notes: Heb “are.” Another option is to translate, “There will be seven years of famine.”
verses.commentary:
41:27

NASB, Peshitta
"thin ears"

NKJV
"empty heads"

NRSV, JPSOA
"empty ears"

TEV
"thin heads of grain"

NJB
"shriveled ears of grain"

LXX
"thin and blasted ears"

The Hebrew words for

- thin (BDB 210), הדקות

- empty (BDB 938), הרקות

The letters d (ד) and r (ר) are often
confused. The UBS Preliminary and Interim Report on the Hebrew Old Testament Text Project (1979, p. 62)
gives "thin" a "B" rating (some doubt).

verses.zh: 这就是我对法老所说，　神已将所要做的事显明给法老了。
verses.en: This is just what I told[NOTE:1] Pharaoh: God has shown Pharaoh what he is about to do.
notes: Heb “it is the word that I spoke.”

verses.zh: 埃及遍地必来七个大丰年，
verses.en: Seven years of great abundance are coming throughout the whole land of Egypt.

verses.zh: 随后又要来七个荒年，甚至在埃及地都忘了先前的丰收，全地必被饥荒所灭。
verses.en: But seven years of famine will occur[NOTE:1] after them, and all the abundance will be forgotten in the land of Egypt. The famine will devastate[NOTE:2] the land.
notes: The perfect with the vav consecutive continues the time frame of the preceding participle, which has an imminent future nuance here.
The Hebrew verb כָּלָה (kalah) in the Piel stem means “to finish, to destroy, to bring an end to.” The severity of the famine will ruin the land of Egypt.

verses.zh: 因那以后的饥荒甚大，便不觉得先前的丰收了。
verses.en: The previous abundance of the land will not be remembered[NOTE:1] because of the famine that follows, for the famine will be very severe.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “known.”
Or “heavy.”

verses.zh: 至于法老两回做梦，是因　神命定这事，而且必速速成就。
verses.en: The dream was repeated to Pharaoh[NOTE:1] because the matter has been decreed[NOTE:2] by God, and God will make it happen soon.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “and concerning the repeating of the dream to Pharaoh two times.” The Niphal infinitive here is the object of the preposition; it is followed by the subjective genitive “of the dream.”
Heb “established.”
The clause combines a participle and an infinitive construct: God “is hurrying…to do it,” meaning he is going to do it soon.
verses.commentary:
41:32 "the matter is determined by God, and God will quickly bring it about" Joseph is asserting his
God's power and foreknowledge related to events in Egypt. The Egyptian magicians (cf. Exodus 7-8), and by
implication the Egyptian gods, were not able to know it or stop it.

YHWH later used the plagues of the Exodus to also depreciate the Egyptian pantheon. YHWH
wants Egyptians to know Him!

verses.zh: 所以，法老当拣选一个有聪明有智慧的人，派他治理埃及地。
verses.en: “So now Pharaoh should look[NOTE:1] for a wise and discerning man[NOTE:2] and give him authority[NOTE:3] over all the land of Egypt.
notes: Heb “let Pharaoh look.” The jussive form expresses Joseph’s advice to Pharaoh.
Heb “a man discerning and wise.” The order of the terms is rearranged in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “and let him set him.”
verses.commentary:
41:33-36 In these verses Joseph gives his wise understanding of what should be done to prepare for
the abundance and then severe famine.

Notice the VERBALS.

- "let Pharaoh look for a man, discerning and wise," Gen. 41:33, BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal
JUSSIVE

- "set him over the land of Egypt," Gen. 41:33, BDB 1011, KB 1483, Qal IMPERFECT
used in a JUSSIVE sense

- "let Pharaoh take action," Gen. 41:34, BDB 793, KB 889, Qal IMPERFECT used in
a JUSSIVE sense

- "appoint overseers," Gen. 41:34, BDB 823, KB 955, Hiphil JUSSIVE

- "let him exact a fifth of the produce of the land," Gen. 41:34, BDB 332, KB 331, Piel
PERFECT with waw used in a JUSSIVE sense (NASB)

- "let them gather all the food," Gen. 41:35, BDB 867, KB 1062, Qal IMPERFECT
used in a JUSSIVE sense

- "store up the grain," Gen. 41:35, BDB 840, KB 999, Qal IMPERFECT used in a
JUSSIVE sense

- "let them guard it," Gen. 41:35, BDB 1036, KB 1581, Qal PERFECT with waw
used in a JUSSIVE sense (NASB)

- "let the food become as a reserve," Gen. 41:36, BDB 224, KB 242, Qal PERFECT
with waw used in a JUSSIVE sense (there are three Qal PERFECTS
functioning as JUSSIVES in this context)

- also note the phrase "it will be very severe" of Gen. 41:31

41:33 It should be noted that YHWH's revealed forecast of seven years of abundance and then seven
years of famine (which no one can affect, yet here it is not a judgment from God, but a weather cycle in a
fallen world) can only be dealt with by purposeful, planned human action. This interconnect of God's
sovereignty/knowledge and human activity is characteristic of the Bible. Both are crucial (cf. Exodus 3,
God's knowledge/action in Gen. 41:7-9, but Moses' need to respond in Gen. 41:10-12).

verses.zh: 法老当这样行，又派官员管理这地。当七个丰年的时候，征收埃及地的五分之一，
verses.en: Pharaoh should do[NOTE:1] this—he should appoint[NOTE:2] officials[NOTE:3] throughout the land to collect one-fifth of the produce of the land of Egypt[NOTE:4] during the seven years of abundance.
notes: The imperfect verbal form has an obligatory nuance here. Smr has a jussive form here, “and let [Pharaoh] do.”
Heb “and let him appoint.” The jussive form expresses Joseph’s advice to Pharaoh.
Heb “appointees.” The noun is a cognate accusative of the preceding verb. Since “appoint appointees” would be redundant in English, the term “officials” was used in the translation instead.
Heb “and he shall collect a fifth of the land of Egypt.” The language is figurative (metonymy); it means what the land produces, i.e., the harvest.
verses.commentary:
41:34 "and let him exact a fifth of the produce of the land of Egypt" Notice that the phrase
"of the produce" is in italics, which means it is not in the Hebrew text. Therefore, the VERB
"exact a fifth" (BDB 332, KB 331, Piel PERFECT with waw) can refer to a taxation
of 20%, which we learn was common in the Egyptian literature, or it might refer to a dividing of the land of
Egypt into five administrative districts (AB, p. 313).

Some commentators think the VERB is coming from the PASSIVE
PARTICIPLE חמשׁ (BDB 332), which means "armed" or "equipped" (cf. Jos. 1:14; 4:12; Jdg. 7:11, AB, p. 313). This is followed by the JPSOA, "organize the land of Egypt."

verses.zh: 叫他们把将来丰年一切的粮食聚敛起来，积蓄五谷，收存在各城里做食物，归于法老的手下。
verses.en: They should gather all the excess food[NOTE:1] during these good years that are coming. By Pharaoh’s authority[NOTE:2] they should store up grain so the cities will have food,[NOTE:3] and they should preserve it.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “all the food.”
Heb “under the hand of Pharaoh.”
Heb “[for] food in the cities.” The noun translated “food” is an adverbial accusative in the sentence.
The perfect with vav (ו) consecutive carries the same force as the sequence of jussives before it.

verses.zh: 所积蓄的粮食可以防备埃及地将来的七个荒年，免得这地被饥荒所灭。」
verses.en: This food should be held in storage for the land in preparation for the seven years of famine that will occur throughout the land of Egypt. In this way the land will survive the famine.”[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “and the land will not be cut off in the famine.”
verses.commentary:
41:36 "so that the land may not perish during the famine" The term "land" (BDB 75) is functioning as
a metaphor for the people and government of Egypt.

verses.zh: 法老和他一切臣仆都以这事为妙。
verses.en: This advice made sense to Pharaoh and all his officials.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “and the matter was good in the eyes of Pharaoh and in the eyes of all his servants.”

verses.zh: 法老对臣仆说：「像这样的人，有　神的灵在他里头，我们岂能找得着呢？」
verses.en: So Pharaoh asked his officials, “Can we find a man like Joseph,[NOTE:1] one in whom the Spirit of God is present?”[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “like this,” but the referent could be misunderstood to be a man like that described by Joseph in v. 33, rather than Joseph himself. For this reason the proper name “Joseph” has been supplied in the translation.
The rhetorical question expects the answer “No, of course not!”
verses.commentary:
41:38 "a divine spirit" This is translated from the Hebrew words ruach Elohim (BDB 924, and
BDB 43). Notice that Pharaoh uses the same name for God as Joseph has used. This seems to be a common
characterization for one who was able to interpret dreams (cf. Dan. 4:8, 9, 18; 5:11, 14) by non-Hebrews.

verses.zh: 法老对约瑟说：「　神既将这事都指示你，可见没有人像你这样有聪明有智慧。
verses.en: So Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Because God has enabled you to know all this, there is no one as wise and discerning[NOTE:1] as you are!
notes: Heb “as discerning and wise.” The order has been rearranged in the translation for stylistic reasons.

verses.zh: 你可以掌管我的家；我的民都必听从你的话。惟独在宝座上我比你大。」
verses.en: You will oversee my household, and all my people will submit to your commands.[NOTE:1] Only I, the king, will be greater than you.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and at your mouth (i.e., instructions) all my people will kiss.” G. J. Wenham translates this “shall kowtow to your instruction” (Genesis [WBC], 2:395). Although there is some textual support for reading “will be judged, ruled by you,” this is probably an attempt to capture the significance of this word. Wenham lists a number of references where individuals have tried to make connections with other words or expressions—such as a root meaning “order themselves” lying behind “kiss,” or an idiomatic idea of “kiss” meaning “seal the mouth,” and so “be silent and submit to.” See K. A. Kitchen, “The Term Nsq in Genesis 41:40, ” ExpTim 69 (1957): 30; D. S. Sperling, “Genesis 41:40: A New Interpretation,” JANESCU 10 (1978): 113-19.
Heb “only the throne, I will be greater than you.”
verses.commentary:
41:40

NASB
"do homage"

NKJV, Peshitta
"shall be ruled"

NRSV
"shall order themselves"

TEV
"will obey your orders"

NJB
"respect your order"

LXX
"be obedient to your word"

JPSOA
"be directed"

REB
"will respect your every word"

The etymology of this term is uncertain, but it seems to be related to a Hebrew root
which means "kiss upon the mouth" (BDB 676, KB 30, Qal IMPERFECT). It may mean

- "to be obedient" (KB)

- "to kiss the ground as a gesture of homage" (cf. Ps. 2:12)

Egyptians shall honor Joseph's word (lit. "mouth") as they do Pharaoh's (cf. Gen. 41:42,43,44).
He was made Pharaoh's "Grand Vizier."

verses.zh: 法老又对约瑟说：「我派你治理埃及全地。」
verses.en: “See here,” Pharaoh said to Joseph, “I place[NOTE:1] you in authority over all the land of Egypt.”[NOTE:2]
notes: The translation assumes that the perfect verbal form is descriptive of a present action. Another option is to understand it as rhetorical, in which case Pharaoh describes a still future action as if it had already occurred in order to emphasize its certainty. In this case one could translate “I have placed” or “I will place.” The verb נָתַן (natan) is translated here as “to place in authority [over].”
Joseph became the grand vizier of the land of Egypt. See W. A. Ward, “The Egyptian Office of Joseph,” JSS 5 (1960): 144-50; and R. de Vaux, Ancient Israel, 129-31.

verses.zh: 法老就摘下手上打印的戒指，戴在约瑟的手上，给他穿上细麻衣，把金链戴在他的颈项上，
verses.en: Then Pharaoh took his signet ring from his own hand and put it on Joseph’s. He clothed him with fine linen[NOTE:1] clothes and put a gold chain around his neck.
notes: The Hebrew word שֵׁשׁ (shesh) is an Egyptian loanword that describes the fine linen robes that Egyptian royalty wore. The clothing signified Joseph’s rank.
verses.commentary:
41:42 "his signet ring" This is from the same root as the VERB "to sink down" (BDB 371),
which may refer to the official ring sinking down in clay or wax to officially document something
(cf. Esther 3:10,12; 8:8,10).

▣ "clothed him in garments of fine linen" This is another Egyptian loan (BDB 1058 III) word that
refers to the fine white linen worn by the elite classes of Egyptian society.

▣ "put the gold necklace around his neck" This was a symbol of authority throughout Egyptian
history, particularly in the 12th dynasty (cf. Dan. 5:7, 16, 29). All of these details are true of Egypt's
culture of the period. These are eyewitness details!

verses.zh: 又叫约瑟坐他的副车，喝道的在前呼叫说：「跪下。」这样，法老派他治理埃及全地。
verses.en: Pharaoh[NOTE:1] had him ride in the chariot used by his second-in-command,[NOTE:2] and they cried out before him, “Kneel down!”[NOTE:3] So he placed him over all the land of Egypt.
notes: Heb “he”; the referent (Pharaoh) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “and he caused him to ride in the second chariot which was his.”
The verb form appears to be a causative imperative from a verbal root meaning “to kneel.” It is a homonym of the word “bless” (identical in root letters but not related etymologically).
verses.commentary:
41:43 "second chariot" This was a way of referring to Joseph as second in command of Egypt
(i.e., Grand Vizier). The term "second" (BDB 1041) often refers to political or administrative offices
(cf. 1 Sam. 23:17; 2 Kgs. 23:4; 25:18; 1 Chr. 5:12; 15:18; 2 Chr. 28:7; 31:12; Neh. 11:17; Esther 10:3;
Jer. 52:24).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARIOTS

▣

NASB, NKJV, NRSV
"Bow the knee!"

TEV, REB
"Make way!"

NJB, JPSOA
"Abrek!"

Peshitta
"Father and governor!"

The meaning of this Egyptian term ("Abrek," cf. NJB, JPSOA) has been greatly debated. It sounds
like the Hebrew root "to kneel" or "a blessing" (barakh, BDB 138-139). There are several other possible
translations found in Brown, Driver and Briggs (BDB 7). However, the Vulgate, Aquilla's Hebrew translation,
Origen of Alexandria, and the Jewish commentator, Kimchi, all say that it means "to bow the knee," which
sounds like the ancient Hebrew root. This seems to be the best possibility contextually.

Here are BDB and KB options.

- BDB

- prostrate thyself!

- head bowed!

- head of the wise

- rejoice thou!

- thy command is our desire

- vizier (Akkadian root)

- KB

- watch out

- kneel down

verses.zh: 法老对约瑟说：「我是法老，在埃及全地，若没有你的命令，不许人擅自办事（原文是动手动脚）。」
verses.en: Pharaoh also said to Joseph, “I am Pharaoh, but without your permission[NOTE:1] no one[NOTE:2] will move his hand or his foot[NOTE:3] in all the land of Egypt.”
notes: Heb “apart from you.”
Heb “no man,” but here “man” is generic, referring to people in general.
The idiom “lift up hand or foot” means “take any action” here.
verses.commentary:
41:44 "no one shall raise his hand or foot" This is an idiom for "no work or effort shall start or
continue without Joseph's permission." It denotes a total and complete authority.

verses.zh: 法老赐名给约瑟，叫撒发那忒・巴内亚，又将安城的祭司波提非拉的女儿亚西纳给他为妻。约瑟就出去巡行埃及地。
verses.en: Pharaoh gave Joseph the name Zaphenath-Paneah.[NOTE:1] He also gave him Asenath[NOTE:2] daughter of Potiphera, priest of On,[NOTE:3] to be his wife. So Joseph took charge of[NOTE:4] all the land of Egypt.
notes: The meaning of Joseph’s Egyptian name, Zaphenath-Paneah, is uncertain. Many recent commentators have followed the proposal of G. Steindorff that it means “the god has said, ‘he will live’” (“Der Name Josephs Saphenat-Pa‘neach,” ZÄS 31 [1889]: 41-42); others have suggested “the god speaks and lives” (see BDB 861 s.v. צָפְנָת פַּעְנֵחַ); “the man he knows” (J. Vergote, Joseph en Égypte, 145); or “Joseph [who is called] ʾIp-ʿankh” (K. A. Kitchen, NBD3 1262).

The name Asenath may mean “she belongs to the goddess Neit” (see HALOT 74 s.v. אָֽסְנַת). A novel was written at the beginning of the first century entitled Joseph and Asenath, which included a legendary account of the conversion of Asenath to Joseph’s faith in Yahweh. However, all that can be determined from this chapter is that their children received Hebrew names. See also V. Aptowitzer, “Asenath, the Wife of Joseph—a Haggadic Literary-Historical Study,” HUCA 1 (1924): 239-306.
On (also in v. 50) is another name for the city of Heliopolis.
Heb “and he passed through.”
verses.commentary:
41:45 "Then Pharaoh named Joseph Zaphenath-paneah" This is an official title (BDB 861) related to
Pharaoh himself (cf. Gen. 45:8). Pharaoh's naming him may have been a cultural sign of his authority over
Joseph. There have been several proposed etymologies.

- The most popular one has been "the god speaks and he lives," which seems to refer to Pharaoh as
the son of the sun god, Re, or possibly Joseph's God speaks and saves Egypt.

- Another possibility is "he who knows things," which would refer to Joseph as a dream interpreter.

- The JPSOA footnote suggests "creator of life"

▣ "and he gave him Asenath, the daughter of" This is another Egyptian name which means "belongs
to Neith" (BDB 62, cf. Gen. 41:45,50; 46:20), who is the love goddess of the Egyptians.

▣ "Potiphera priest of On" This is another Egyptian name which is a lengthening of the name
Potiphar, found in Gen. 37:36; 39:1. It means "he to whom (Re) gave" (BDB 806). Pharaoh is making Joseph a
part of the elite class of Egypt's society by this marriage to the daughter of an important priest
(BDB 463).

▣ "On" "On" (BDB 58) is the city of the sun god. It is called Heliopolis in Greek and Beth
Shemesh in Hebrew (cf. Jer. 43:13). It was located about seven miles north of Cairo, on the border of
the Land of Goshen.

▣

NASB, NKJV
"and Joseph went forth over the land of Egypt"

NRSV
"Thus Joseph gained authority over the land of Egypt"

TEV
"traveled all over the land"

NJB, Peshitta
"and Joseph began to journey all over Egypt"

REB
"Joseph's authority extended over the whole of Egypt"

JPSOA
"Thus Joseph emerged in charge of the land of Egypt"

This phrase is literally translated in the NASB and NKJV. However, its meaning is
disputed.

- vv. 45 and 46 are parallel, therefore, "traveled over the whole land" (TEV, NJB, NIV)

- in Esther 1:17 this very common VERB "go" or "come" (BDB 422, KB 425, Qal
IMPERFECT), also a Qal IMPERFECT, is used in the sense of
something spreading (i.e., the message about Vasti's defiance). So here Joseph's fame and authority
spread throughout the land (NRSV, REB).

- Because the phrase "over the land" following the VERB is used in Gen. 41:33, 41,
and 43 in connection with Joseph's authority as Vizier, then the VERB here must
refer to that also (JPSOA).

verses.zh: 约瑟见埃及王法老的时候年三十岁。他从法老面前出去，遍行埃及全地。
verses.en: Now Joseph was 30 years old[NOTE:1] when he began serving[NOTE:2] Pharaoh king of Egypt. Joseph was commissioned by[NOTE:3] Pharaoh and was in charge of[NOTE:4] all the land of Egypt.
notes: Heb “a son of thirty years.”
Heb “when he stood before.”
Heb “went out from before.”
Heb “and he passed through all the land of Egypt”; this phrase is interpreted by JPS to mean that Joseph “emerged in charge of the whole land.”
verses.commentary:
41:46 "thirty years old" This is literally "son of thirty years," which is an idiom (cf. Lev. 27:5;
2 Kgs. 8:26; Jer. 52:1).

verses.zh: 七个丰年之内，地的出产极丰极盛（原文是一把一把的），
verses.en: During the seven years of abundance the land produced large, bountiful harvests.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “brought forth by handfuls.”
verses.commentary:
41:47-49 Joseph's dream interpretation was completely accurate. The abundance is accentuated in
several ways.

- seven years of plenty, Gen. 41:47

- the land brought forth abundantly, Gen. 41:47

- stored grain in great abundance, Gen. 41:47, 47

- like the sand of the sea, Gen. 41:49

- until he stopped measuring it for it was beyond measure, Gen. 41:49

verses.zh: 约瑟聚敛埃及地七个丰年一切的粮食，把粮食积存在各城里；各城周围田地的粮食都积存在本城里。
verses.en: Joseph[NOTE:1] collected all the excess food[NOTE:2] in the land of Egypt during the seven years and stored it in the cities.[NOTE:3] In every city he put the food gathered from the fields around it.
notes: Heb “he”; the referent (Joseph) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “all the food.”
Heb “of the seven years which were in the land of Egypt and placed food in the cities.”

verses.zh: 约瑟积蓄五谷甚多，如同海边的沙，无法计算，因为谷不可胜数。
verses.en: Joseph stored up a vast amount of grain, like the sand of the sea,[NOTE:1] until he stopped measuring it because it was impossible to measure.
notes: Heb “and Joseph gathered grain like the sand of the sea, multiplying much.” To emphasize the vast amount of grain he stored up, the Hebrew text modifies the verb “gathered” with an infinitive absolute and an adverb.

verses.zh: 荒年未到以前，安城的祭司波提非拉的女儿亚西纳给约瑟生了两个儿子。
verses.en: Two sons were born to Joseph before the famine came.[NOTE:1] Asenath daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, was their mother.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “before the year of the famine came.”
Heb “gave birth for him.”

verses.zh: 约瑟给长子起名叫玛拿西（就是使之忘了的意思），因为他说：「　神使我忘了一切的困苦和我父的全家。」
verses.en: Joseph named the firstborn Manasseh,[NOTE:1] saying,[NOTE:2] “Certainly[NOTE:3] God has made me forget all my trouble and all my father’s house.”
notes: The name Manasseh (מְנַשֶּׁה, menasheh) describes God’s activity on behalf of Joseph, explaining in general the significance of his change of fortune. The name is a Piel participle, suggesting the meaning “he who brings about forgetfulness.” The Hebrew verb נַשַּׁנִי (nashani) may have been used instead of the normal נִשַּׁנִי (nishani) to provide a closer sound play with the name. The giving of this Hebrew name to his son shows that Joseph retained his heritage and faith; and it shows that a brighter future was in store for him.
The word “saying” has been supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Or “for.”
verses.commentary:
41:51 "Manasseh" This name (BDB 586) is related to the Hebrew VERB "to forget"
(BDB 674, KB 728, Piel PARTICIPLE) by sound similarity. This is specifically related
to the pain involved in the actions of his brothers. Later events in Genesis show that Joseph had not
completely gotten over his brother's hateful betrayal.

verses.zh: 他给次子起名叫以法莲（就是使之昌盛的意思），因为他说：「　神使我在受苦的地方昌盛。」
verses.en: He named the second child Ephraim,[NOTE:1] saying,[NOTE:2] “Certainly[NOTE:3] God has made me fruitful in the land of my suffering.”
notes: The name Ephraim (אֶפְרַיִם, ʾefrayim), a form of the Hebrew verb פָּרָה (parah), means “to bear fruit.” The theme of fruitfulness is connected with this line of the family from Rachel (30:2) on down (see Gen 49:22, Deut 33:13-17, and Hos 13:15). But there is some difficulty with the name “Ephraim” itself. It appears to be a dual, for which F. Delitzsch simply said it meant “double fruitfulness” (New Commentary on Genesis, 2:305). G. J. Spurrell suggested it was a diphthongal pronunciation of a name ending in -an or -am, often thought to be dual suffixes (Notes on the text of the book of Genesis, 334). Many, however, simply connect the name to the territory of Ephraim and interpret it to be “fertile land” (C. Fontinoy, “Les noms de lieux en -ayim dans la Bible,” UF 3 [1971]: 33-40). The dual would then be an old locative ending. There is no doubt that the name became attached to the land in which the tribe settled, and it is possible that is where the dual ending came from, but in this story it refers to Joseph’s God-given fruitfulness.
The word “saying” has been supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Or “for.”
verses.commentary:
41:52 "Ephraim" This name (BDB 68) is related to a term "fruitfulness" or "double fruit" (BDB 826,
cf. Gen. 49:22) by popular wordplay. It is interesting to note that in modern Israel, Jewishness is
determined by the Jewish mother. In reality, these two boys are not really Jewish! They will later become
the half-tribes who will inherit Joseph's double portion and will make up part of the twelve tribes
(i.e., thirteen) of Israel. Levi will not be counted as a tribe for inheritance purposes (cf. Joshua).

verses.zh: 埃及地的七个丰年一完，
verses.en: The seven years of abundance in the land of Egypt came to an end.
verses.commentary:
41:53-57 This explains historically how Pharaoh came to own all the land of Egypt (cf. Gen. 47:20-26).
The Egyptians sold their land to the king to buy grain to feed themselves and their families.

It must be noted that famine would have shown the failure of Egyptian religion (i.e., sun god,
fertility gods, and the Nile itself) to be able to deliver Egypt, but YHWH could!

verses.zh: 七个荒年就来了。正如约瑟所说的，各地都有饥荒；惟独埃及全地有粮食。
verses.en: Then the seven years of famine began,[NOTE:1] just as Joseph had predicted. There was famine in all the other lands, but throughout the land of Egypt there was food.
notes: Heb “began to arrive.”

verses.zh: 及至埃及全地有了饥荒，众民向法老哀求粮食，法老对他们说：「你们往约瑟那里去，凡他所说的，你们都要做。」
verses.en: When all the land of Egypt experienced the famine, the people cried out to Pharaoh for food. Pharaoh said to all the people of Egypt,[NOTE:1] “Go to Joseph and do whatever he tells you.”
notes: Heb “to all Egypt.” The name of the country is used by metonymy for the inhabitants.

verses.zh: 当时饥荒遍满天下，约瑟开了各处的仓，粜粮给埃及人；在埃及地饥荒甚大。
verses.en: While the famine was over all the earth,[NOTE:1] Joseph opened the storehouses[NOTE:2] and sold grain to the Egyptians. The famine was severe throughout the land of Egypt.
notes: Or “over the entire land”; Heb “over all the face of the earth.” The disjunctive clause is circumstantial-temporal to the next clause.
The MT reads “he opened all that was in [or “among”] them.” The translation follows the reading of the LXX and Syriac versions.
verses.commentary:
41:56

NASB, NKJV, NRSV, TEV, Peshitta, Vulgate
"all the storehouses"

NJB, LXX, REB
"all the granaries"

JPSOA
"all that was within"

The Hebrew text is literally translated by JPSOA. The UBS Text Project, p. 64, gives
this option a "B" rating (some doubt). It can refer to

- all the places where Joseph stored the grain

- all the places where the Egyptians could buy grain throughout the land

verses.zh: 各地的人都往埃及去，到约瑟那里籴粮，因为天下的饥荒甚大。
verses.en: People from every country[NOTE:1] came to Joseph in Egypt to buy grain because the famine was severe throughout the earth.
notes: Heb “all the earth,” which refers here (by metonymy) to the people of the earth. Note that the following verb is plural in form, indicating that the inhabitants of the earth are in view.
verses.commentary:
41:57 This verse describes the terrible drought and famine over the whole Near East and
Mediterranean area. Many nations came to Egypt to buy food. Joseph saved

- Egypt

- many other surrounding people groups

- especially the chosen family of Jacob!

God's providence functions on several levels!

Note the hyperbole in the phrase "all the earth." This is parallel to the phrase used in
Genesis 6-7 about the extent of the flood (cf. Gen. 7:19, ארצ, 'eres, BDB 75; Bernard Ramm,
The Christian View of Science and Scripture, pp. 119-178, esp. p. 164).

EARTH

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are
responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You,
the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this
section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

- List all of the Egyptian loan words in this chapter and the uniquely Egyptian customs.

- Describe magicians and their function in the Ancient Near East.

- List all of the ways that Joseph's new position is described in Gen. 41:41-44.

- What is the meaning of the names of Joseph's sons and what is their significance (Gen. 41:50-52)?

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: GENESIS 41:1-8

1Now it happened at the end of two full years that Pharaoh had a dream, and behold, he was standing by the Nile. 2And lo, from the Nile there came up seven cows, sleek and fat; and they grazed in the marsh grass. 3Then behold, seven other cows came up after them from the Nile, ugly and gaunt, and they stood by the other cows on the bank of the Nile. 4The ugly and gaunt cows ate up the seven sleek and fat cows. Then Pharaoh awoke. 5He fell asleep and dreamed a second time; and behold, seven ears of grain came up on a single stalk, plump and good. 6Then behold, seven ears, thin and scorched by the east wind, sprouted up after them. 7The thin ears swallowed up the seven plump and full ears. Then Pharaoh awoke, and behold, it was a dream. 8Now in the morning his spirit was troubled, so he sent and called for all the magicians of Egypt, and all its wise men. And Pharaoh told them his dreams, but there was no one who could interpret them to Pharaoh.
